section.title: Hosea's Marriage and Children
section.sectionRationale: The book opens not with a sermon but with a marriage. God tells Hosea to take an unfaithful wife and to name their children with names of judgment, turning the prophet's own household into a living picture of the LORD and faithless Israel. The chapter moves from three names of doom to a stunning promise of reversal.
section.thesis: God enacts His message through Hosea's family: a wayward wife pictures wayward Israel, three ominous names announce scattering, no mercy, and no covenant, yet the chapter ends with those very sentences overturned by grace.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the superscription; the command to marry Gomer and name Jezreel; the births of Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi; and the sudden promise that reverses every name.

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to Hosea son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam son of Jehoash, king of Israel.

When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, He told him, “Go, take a prostitute as your wife and have children of adultery, because this land is flagrantly prostituting itself by departing from the LORD.”
So Hosea went and married Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son.
Then the LORD said to Hosea, “Name him {{jezreel|Jezreel}}, for soon I will bring the bloodshed of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will put an end to the kingdom of Israel.
And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.”

Gomer again conceived and gave birth to a daughter, and the LORD said to Hosea, “Name her {{loRuhamah|Lo-ruhamah}}, for I will no longer have {{racham|compassion}} on the house of Israel, that I should ever forgive them.
Yet I will have compassion on the house of Judah, and I will save them, not by bow or sword or war, not by horses and cavalry, but by the LORD their God.”
After she had weaned Lo-ruhamah, Gomer conceived and gave birth to a son.
And the LORD said, “Name him {{loAmmi|Lo-ammi}}, for you are not My people, and I am not your God.”

units.label: The promise that reverses the names

verses.text: Yet the number of the Israelites will be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or counted. And it will happen that in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
Then the people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together, and they will appoint for themselves one leader, and will go up out of the land. For great will be the day of Jezreel.

jezreel.gloss: Jezreel means God sows. It was the valley where Jehu's dynasty shed blood to seize the throne, so the name first sounds like judgment on that house. Yet the same word can mean God plants a people in the land, and by verse 11 it turns into a word of hope, the great day of Jezreel.

loRuhamah.gloss: Lo-ruhamah means she has not received mercy, or not pitied. The name announces that God will withhold His tender compassion from faithless Israel. It is built on the root racham, the deep, motherly mercy that God says He will no longer show, until He reverses it in chapter 2.

loAmmi.gloss: Lo-ammi means not My people. It is the undoing of the covenant formula, I will be your God and you will be My people. To name a child this is to declare the covenant bond severed, the most devastating word Israel could hear, and the one the gospel most gloriously reverses.

racham.gloss: To have compassion, to show tender mercy. The word is related to the Hebrew for womb, picturing the visceral, protective love of a parent. Its removal in the name Lo-ruhamah is the withdrawal of that mercy; its return in chapter 2 is the heart of God's restoring grace.

basic.context: Hosea preached to the northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades before Assyria destroyed it. God gave him a shocking assignment: marry an unfaithful woman and let his family become a sermon. Each child receives a name that spells out the coming judgment, scattering, no mercy, and no longer My people. Then, without warning, God promises to turn every one of those names around.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a true account of a prophet's life used as a sign. People debate how much of the marriage is literal, but the meaning is plain: Israel has been unfaithful to God like a spouse who strays, and judgment is coming. Yet the last two verses are pure promise, and the New Testament quotes them as fulfilled when God brings in a people from all nations.
basic.originalLanguages: The three names carry the message. Jezreel means God sows, first a place of bloodshed, later a word of planting and hope. Lo-ruhamah means not pitied, built on racham, the tender, womb-like mercy of God. Lo-ammi means not My people, the reversal of the covenant promise. In verse 10 all of this flips: they will be called sons of the living God.
basic.typology: Hosea acting out God's message with his own family points to the God who does not merely speak His love but enacts it, ultimately in the incarnation. The reversal of not My people into My people is the pattern by which God brings outsiders into His family through Christ.
basic.christ: Paul quotes verse 10 in Romans 9 to explain how God calls a people from among the Gentiles, and Peter echoes it in 1 Peter 2:10, once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God. The one leader Israel and Judah gather under, verse 11, points to the Messiah, great David's greater Son, under whom the scattered are gathered.
basic.god: We meet a God who feels His people's betrayal as a wounded husband, who will not wink at sin, yet whose final word is not rejection but restoration. His mercy outlasts His judgment; He announces the reversal before the judgment has even fallen.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 9:25-26 and 1 Peter 2:10 both quote this chapter to describe the church. 2 Kings 10 records the bloodshed of Jezreel. Exodus 6:7 gives the covenant formula that these names undo and then restore.
basic.oneStory: The chapter sets the whole book in motion: a holy God bound in covenant love to an unfaithful people, judgment that is real, and mercy that is greater still. The promise that not My people will become My people runs straight to Christ, who gathers a countless family, Jew and Gentile, under one Head.

context.literary:
Hosea 1 is a compact narrative with a single hinge. Verses 2 to 9 are built as three births in a steady rhythm: she conceived, she bore, the LORD said name him. Each naming speech gives a reason introduced by 'for' (verses 4, 6, 9), and each reason is heavier than the one before. The first sentence announces an end to a dynasty, the second withdraws mercy from the northern kingdom, and the third cancels the covenant formula itself. Then verses 10 and 11 begin with the little word 'yet,' and the whole movement turns. Everything in verses 2 to 9 is the negation of a promise; everything in verses 10 and 11 is the same promise given back.

The chapter is also written to be heard as a reversal of the Sinai bond. 'You are not My people, and I am not your God' undoes the covenant sentence of Exodus 6:7 and Leviticus 26:12. The prophet's own household becomes the vehicle, which is why the narrative is told with so little comment. There is no description of Hosea's feelings and no speech from Gomer. The narrator wants the reader to look at the children, and at the names, the way Israel's neighbours would have looked at them as they were called across the courtyard.

The first verse is the book's heading, giving the prophet's father and a list of kings. Judah's four kings stand first and Israel's single king stands last, an unusual order for a prophet addressed mainly to the north. It signals that Hosea's word was preserved and read in Judah after the north had fallen, and that Judah is meant to take the warning. Verse 2 opens with a phrase that can be read as 'the beginning of the LORD's speaking through Hosea.' The book therefore starts with the marriage, and everything that follows in chapters 4 to 14 is to be read in its light.
context.historical:
The kings of verse 1 stretch across roughly half a century of the eighth century BC. Jeroboam son of Jehoash, the second of that name, ruled the north through a long, prosperous reign. Trade and territory expanded, and the wealth fed a confident religion of shrines and festivals. But the prosperity covered deep rot. Within about thirty years of Jeroboam's death the kingdom saw a string of short reigns and murders, and in 722 BC Samaria fell to Assyria. The last king of Israel was another Hoshea, the son of Elah, 2 Kings 17:1, a sad coincidence of names with the prophet whose name means salvation.

Jezreel is the key to verse 4. It was the fertile plain and royal town in the north where Ahab's family had a palace and where Naboth's vineyard lay, 1 Kings 21:1-4. It was also the place where Jehu came to power. At the prophets' word Jehu killed Joram, Jezebel and the house of Ahab there, 2 Kings 9:30-37, and he went on to a wider slaughter at Samaria. God rewarded the obedient part with a promise that four generations of Jehu's sons would sit on the throne, 2 Kings 10:30. Those four came and went, and Zechariah, the fourth, was cut down by Shallum after six months, 2 Kings 15:10-12. The Jezreel that had been the birthplace of the dynasty would be the place of its reckoning.

The name Gomer daughter of Diblaim is given without any comment about her family, which is itself a mark that these are real people in a real marriage. Naming children as signs was a known prophetic practice. Isaiah named his sons Shear-jashub and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, Isaiah 7:3 and 8:3-4, and Jeremiah was told not to marry at all, Jeremiah 16:2. In each case the household carried the message.
context.canonical:
Hosea opens the Book of the Twelve, the scroll of the Minor Prophets, and in the Hebrew canon it was counted as one book with the other eleven. Its marriage language sets the metaphor that nearly every later prophet will use. The covenant at Sinai was already a marriage of sorts, and the warning against 'prostituting themselves' to other gods is found in Exodus 34:15-16. Hosea gives that thread its fullest narrative form, and it is picked up by Jeremiah, where the LORD remembers 'the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride,' Jeremiah 2:2, by Ezekiel's long account of a foundling girl who becomes a bride and a harlot in Ezekiel 16, and by Isaiah, where the Maker becomes the husband, Isaiah 54:5.

Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 are among the most widely quoted lines in the New Testament. Paul takes both in Romans 9:25-26 and applies them to Gentiles as well as Jews who are called in Christ. Peter reaches for the same words in 1 Peter 2:10, writing to churches whose members were once outside the covenant: 'Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.' The apostles saw that the God who gathered the lost sheep of Israel was doing in Christ what Hosea had sworn He would do.

The cluster in 1:10 and 1:11 also feeds the prophetic hope for a reunited people under one head, later spelled out in Ezekiel 37:21-22, and the hope of a seed too many to number, which comes back to the promise to Abraham in Genesis 22:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hosea wanted the first hearers to feel the marriage before they understood it. A prophet's household was public life, and the names in this chapter would have been called aloud in the street. Every time a neighbour shouted for the little girl or the boy, the sermon was preached again. The point was to make a nation who thought they were safe feel what their idolatry looked like from God's side, as betrayal inside a covenant.

He also meant to remove two false comforts. One was the belief that Jehu's dynasty was secure because its founder had once served God's purpose. The other was the belief that the covenant was a possession that could not be cancelled. The word 'not' is placed on the people with deliberate shock: not pitied, not mine. Yet the author does not leave the hearers in despair. He places the promise of verses 10 and 11 within the same chapter and almost the same breath, so that the judgment is never heard apart from the pledge. The aim is repentance that runs toward a God who has already said what He will do, and a hope that rests on His oath and not on Israel's merit.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what the LORD told Hosea to do and what happened; it does not make the command a model. No one is told to marry in order to dramatise a message, and the name of a child is not a tool for sending judgments. The sign was unique to this prophet at this hour, just as Isaiah's walking about unclothed or Ezekiel's lying on his side were unique to them.

What continues to apply is the reality that the signs picture. Covenant love is costly, and a people can treat the God who has loved them as a rival to be replaced. Believers are also meant to take the opposite pole of the chapter as their own: the God who says 'not My people' is the God who reverses it. The chapter further warns against reading privileged status as safety, since ancestry in the covenant community, like Jehu's throne, does not shield from judgment. At the same time Hosea 1:10 invites those who feel outside to hear that the place where they were told 'not My people' is the very place where they will be called sons.

debates.question: Was Hosea's marriage a literal event, or a vision or parable?

views.label: A real marriage with a real woman
views.case: The text gives the name of the wife and her father and records the births and the naming in plain narrative sequence. Nothing in the language signals a vision, and the children's names, spoken in real life, carried force because the family was real. Most modern commentators and the weight of the church's reading take this line.

views.label: A vision or literary parable
views.case: Some older interpreters, finding it hard to think God would command such a marriage, took the account as a vision or as a story told for effect. They point to the symbolic names and to the way chapters 2 and 3 slide between wife and nation.

debates.bearing: The passage is told as history, and the best reading takes it so. Even if a reader leans another way, the doctrinal point is unchanged: Israel's idolatry is a betrayal of the one who loved first.

debates.question: How can God judge Jehu's house for the bloodshed of Jezreel when He had commanded Jehu to strike Ahab's house?

views.label: Jehu went beyond his commission
views.case: God's word to Jehu in 2 Kings 9:7 was to strike down Ahab's house. Jehu went further, killing the forty two relatives of Ahaziah of Judah, 2 Kings 10:12-14, and he never turned from the golden calves, 2 Kings 10:29-31. His zeal served himself as much as the LORD.

views.label: Jezreel names the dynasty's whole record of violence
views.case: Later kings of Jehu's line kept to the same sin of Jeroboam, and the throne was kept by blood. On this view 'the bloodshed of Jezreel' sums up a house built on violence, which now falls by violence, as Zechariah's death shows.

debates.bearing: Both views grant that God can use a human act for His purpose and still hold the actor to account. God was just in using Jehu and just in judging the motives and later conduct of his line.

debates.question: What does 'go up out of the land' mean in verse 11?

views.label: Return from exile
views.case: The verb 'go up' belongs to the exodus and pilgrimage vocabulary of the Old Testament. The scattered people will be gathered and will go up from the lands where they were driven, a second exodus under one head.

views.label: Spring up from the ground
views.case: The verb can be used of plants coming up, and the verse ends by naming Jezreel, God sows. Some read a harvest image: the people shoot up like crops from the field the LORD sows.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart, since both describe a people brought out of death into new life by God's own doing.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 contains an intensified construction. The BSB's 'flagrantly prostituting itself' renders an infinitive placed next to its finite verb, literally 'prostituting, the land prostitutes.' The same device marks the very strong statements in the Torah, as in 'dying you shall die.' The prophet's accusation is therefore not that Israel has strayed a little but that the whole land is steeped in unfaithfulness. The wife God tells Hosea to take is described by a phrase that means a woman of prostitutions, and the children by a matching phrase, children of prostitutions. The plural of intensity is used for what is complete and habitual, not a single act.

The name Jezreel in verses 4 and 5 and again in verse 11 is built from the verb zara, to sow, the same root as the noun for seed in the Genesis promises. The footnote to verse 4 gives 'God sows,' and the BSB repeats it at verses 11 and 22. The name is set up to function as a double sign. In verse 4 it is the place of bloodshed. In verse 11 and in 2:22-23, the sound of the same name becomes a promise of sowing, a harvest of people. The word is left unchanged and its meaning is turned.

Lo-ruhamah, in verse 6, is the feminine passive of the verb racham, the footnote saying 'she has not received mercy.' The verb is closely related to the Hebrew word for womb, so that mercy has a sound of the tenderness of a mother toward the child of her body. The clause that follows is notoriously difficult. The BSB has 'that I should ever forgive them,' using the verb nasa, to lift or carry. The same words can be taken to mean 'I will utterly take them away,' which is how some older English versions read it. Either way, the sentence says mercy is withdrawn from the northern kingdom, while verse 7 sets Judah apart with the same verb for compassion.

Lo-ammi, in verse 9, closes the series. The footnote says the Hebrew is 'I am not yours.' Many readers hear in that phrase an echo of the divine self-declaration of Exodus 3:14, 'I AM WHO I AM,' as though the LORD were saying He would no longer be 'I am' for them. The echo is a suggestion, not a certainty, but the covenant reversal is beyond doubt: the Exodus 6:7 pledge, 'I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God,' is cancelled clause by clause.

In verse 10 the phrase 'sons of the living God' uses a name for God, the living one, that sets Him against dead idols. The Hebrew for 'leader' in verse 11 is literally 'head,' the same word used for a chief or a ruler, and the unusual choice leaves the character of that head open until chapter 3 names him as David their king.

typology.type: The prophet's family as a living sign
typology.fulfillment: Hosea does not only speak a message; his household becomes the message. Other prophets used acted signs, Isaiah 20:2-3 and Ezekiel 4:1-3, but none is so bound to a prophet's love and shame. The correspondence is that the LORD is the wounded husband and Israel the wife who strays. The escalation comes when the Word becomes flesh and does not merely act out the message but enters the family of the unfaithful, born of a woman, Galatians 4:4. The type falls short because Hosea's grief was that of a man bearing another's guilt in a figure; Christ bears it in fact.

The name that meant bloodshed in 1:4 turns into the name of a harvest in 1:11 and 2:22-23. This foreshadows a gathering of people from beyond Israel into God's field. Paul takes the promise of 1:10 in Romans 9:25-26 to include Gentiles called in Christ, and Peter tells scattered churches that they are now God's people, 1 Peter 2:10. The sowing is accomplished in the death of Christ, who said that a grain of wheat must fall into the earth and die to bear much fruit, John 12:24. The type is incomplete until the nations are gathered in the last day, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: Judah saved not by bow or sword
typology.fulfillment: Verse 7 promises deliverance for Judah without weapons, 'by the LORD their God.' It was seen in part when the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp in the days of Hezekiah, 2 Kings 19:35. It points ahead to a salvation that the Lord Himself works, not one achieved by human arms. Christ refuses the sword in Gethsemane and tells Pilate that His kingdom is not of this world, John 18:36. The type falls short because the rescue of Jerusalem was a rescue from an earthly army, while Christ's rescue is from sin and death.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ by promise. Verses 10 and 11 describe a people no longer scattered, gathered under one leader. The prophets keep that figure in view, and the LORD says through Jeremiah that His people will serve Him and 'David their king, whom I will raise up for them,' Jeremiah 30:9. In Ezekiel 37:21-22 one king is set over a reunited nation. The New Testament identifies that king as Jesus, who sits on the throne of David, and Peter's quoting of Hosea in 1 Peter 2:10 belongs to a letter that sees the people of the Messiah as the gathered flock.

It points to Christ by pattern. Hosea is asked to name a child 'not My people,' to carry the weight of a message to people who have turned from God. Jesus took on something much heavier. Paul says that 'God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5. The one who could say 'I am' with full right entered the family of those who had broken covenant, and in His death He bore the curse of the law, Galatians 3:13. The rejection that Hosea's children announced falls on Him, so that 'not My people' becomes 'sons of the living God.' Paul can quote verse 10 of Hosea in Romans 9:26 because the adoption of the formerly estranged has been accomplished in the Son.

It also points to Christ through the name of the prophet himself. Hoshea means salvation, from the same root as Joshua, and Moses gave that name its longer form in Numbers 13:16. Jesus carries the same name in its Greek form, Matthew 1:21, 'for He will save His people from their sins.' The prophet whose name means salvation is overtaken by the One who is salvation, and the people who bore a label of rejection are redeemed by Him.

The counsel of caution is that Hosea is not simply a type of Christ in his marriage. He is a prophet and sinner like his hearers, and the larger pattern is that the LORD Himself is the husband. The New Testament writers never turn Gomer's children into allegories for Jesus. They take the reversal of verse 10 as the promise that Christ fulfils.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who stands in a relationship, not behind a screen. He speaks of Israel as a wife, of Himself as a husband, and of the breaking of the bond as a wound. His judgment is therefore not the cold response of a distant lawgiver but the response of a covenant partner whose love has been scorned. This is as far from the picture of an impassive deity as the Bible goes, and yet it never makes God weak: the one who is wounded is also the one who controls the kings, the armies and the valleys.

God is sovereign over history. In verse 4 He reaches back to an event a century earlier and fixes a reckoning upon a dynasty. In verse 5 He promises to break Israel's bow, the symbol of her military pride, and in verse 7 He promises a salvation that will not depend on weapons at all. Nations rise and fall at His word, and the same Lord who judged the northern house decides when and how the house of Judah is spared.

God is just. He counts the cost of bloodshed and will not let it pass because it came to a successful end. Jehu was used by God, yet God does not call a good result a justification for violence done in a divided heart. The withdrawal of mercy in verse 6 and the cancelling of the covenant name in verse 9 are measured by the length and depth of Israel's refusal.

God is also faithful beyond Israel's faithlessness. The most striking feature of the chapter is that the same mouth that says 'not My people' says 'sons of the living God.' The reversal is not given because the people have done anything to deserve it; verse 10 simply begins with 'yet.' The grounds lie in the LORD's own purpose to bring the promise to Abraham to completion, the multitude that cannot be counted, Genesis 22:17. His word of promise stands above His word of judgment.

For worship, this chapter teaches us to bring both terms together. Fear of the LORD takes the 'not' seriously, and comfort in the LORD takes the 'yet' seriously. A people who sing the praise of the living God ought to remember that they were once called by another name, and that He changed it.

crossReferences.note: God's promise to Jehu that four generations of his sons would reign. It explains the sharpness of Hosea 1:4, since the dynasty's end was foreseen and fixed. The promise ran its four generations and then closed.

Shallum strikes down Zechariah, Jehu's great great grandson, and takes the throne. The account shows the fulfilment of 'put an end to the kingdom' in the very house of Jehu, and shows how quickly the north's stability collapsed after Jeroboam II.

Naboth's vineyard at Jezreel, the scene of Ahab's covetous theft. Jezreel is thus a place soaked in royal violence and stolen inheritance, which makes it a fitting name for the bloodshed the LORD will avenge on a house that continued to rule by blood.

Isaiah names his son Maher-shalal-hash-baz as a sign that Assyria will take the wealth of Damascus and Samaria. It is a close parallel to Hosea's children, showing that a prophet's household can be a public warning in the same decades.

The covenant formula spoken in Egypt: 'I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God.' Lo-ammi in Hosea 1:9 reverses it clause by clause, which shows that the children's names are about the covenant itself and not only about politics.

The angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp in Hezekiah's days. It is the closest narrative to Hosea 1:7, where Judah is saved without bow, sword or cavalry, and shows that the promise was kept in the generation Hosea's heading names.

The oath to Abraham that his descendants would be like the sand on the seashore. Hosea 1:10 draws the same image, which means the multitude beyond counting is not a new promise but the old one still standing after the covenant has been broken.

Paul quotes Hosea 2:23 and 1:10 together to show that God's calling reaches those who were not His people. He applies the reversal to Gentiles as well as Jews, which opens the full meaning of 'sons of the living God' in Christ.

Peter uses the pair, not a people now a people, no mercy now mercy, in plain summary of what Hosea's two daughter and son names promise. He tells scattered Christians that the names have been undone for them.

God promises to gather Israel from the nations and make them one nation under one king, no more divided. It is the clearest later commentary on Hosea 1:11, where Judah and Israel are brought together under one head.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is that God made a people for Himself in the garden, lost them, and then set out to bring them home. Hosea 1 stands at a low point of that story, where a whole kingdom is told that it has lost its place in the covenant. It looks back to Eden and to the first marriage, where God joined humanity to Himself and to each other, and it looks back to Sinai, where He took Israel as a bride and gave her the law as a marriage contract. When Israel prostitutes herself with other gods, she repeats Adam's choice to believe another voice.

The chapter also looks back to the promise to Abraham. The multitude as numerous as the sand cannot be reached if the people are cut off, yet the LORD says it will be. The promise made in Genesis is still alive in Hosea's grim hour, and the whole book will keep returning to it. The lost sheep will become many, the barren will bear, and the divided will be one.

Looking forward, the chapter prepares the way for the exile, in which the northern tribes are carried away and Judah is taken after them. It prepares for the long wait for the gathered people under one head. It prepares for the coming of the Son who is called out of Egypt, Matthew 2:15, quoting Hosea 11:1, and who gathers the scattered children of God. In the church, the apostles read the names reversed: those who were not a people are now the people of God, 1 Peter 2:10.

The story ends where Hosea 2 and Revelation meet. The Bible closes with a bride coming down out of heaven, 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2, and with no one called 'not My people' any more. Jezreel's sowing has come to its harvest, the mercy withdrawn has been given in full, and the voice from the throne says that God will dwell with them. The names Hosea gave his children are not the last word. Every one of them is spoken over again in the new creation, and each of them is answered.

quiz.q: Why did God tell Hosea to marry an unfaithful woman?

options.text: To make his marriage a living picture of the LORD's covenant with unfaithful Israel.
options.note: Verse 2 ties the marriage directly to a land prostituting itself by departing from the LORD.

options.text: To teach Hosea patience through personal hardship.
options.note: There was real cost to Hosea, but the stated purpose is the prophetic sign, not personal growth.

options.text: Because no faithful woman was available to the prophet.
options.note: The text gives no such reason; the marriage is a deliberate sign from God.

options.text: To show that God approves of unfaithfulness.
options.note: The opposite is true; the marriage exposes the horror of unfaithfulness to God.

quiz.q: What do the three children's names announce?

options.text: Coming judgment: bloodshed at Jezreel, no more mercy, and no longer My people.
options.note: Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, and Lo-ammi each spell out an aspect of judgment on Israel.

options.text: Only future blessing and prosperity for Israel.
options.note: Blessing comes at the end, but the names themselves are names of judgment.

options.text: The names of Israel's future kings.
options.note: They are sign-names about the nation's covenant standing, not royal names.

options.text: That God had forgotten His people entirely.
options.note: The chapter ends by promising restoration, so God has not forgotten them.

quiz.q: How does the chapter reverse its own names of judgment?

options.text: It promises that not My people will be called sons of the living God, and the scattered will be gathered.
options.note: Verses 10 and 11 overturn Lo-ammi and Jezreel into hope.

options.text: It says the judgment was only a misunderstanding.
options.note: The judgment is real; grace overturns it rather than cancelling that it was deserved.

options.text: It removes all consequences immediately.
options.note: The reversal is a future promise; the judgment still falls in history.

options.text: It ends with no hope at all.
options.note: The chapter ends on a strong note of hope and restoration.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament use Hosea 1:10?

options.text: Paul and Peter apply it to God calling a people, including Gentiles, into His family in Christ.
options.note: Romans 9:25-26 and 1 Peter 2:10 cite Hosea to describe the church.

options.text: It is treated only as a prediction about the modern state of Israel.
options.note: It concerns the people of God gathered in Christ, which the apostles apply to the church.

options.text: It is never referenced in the New Testament.
options.note: It is quoted directly by both Paul and Peter.

options.text: It is used to prove the covenant is permanently cancelled.
options.note: It is used to show mercy and inclusion, the very opposite of cancellation.

quiz.q: What do we learn about God from this opening chapter?

options.text: He feels betrayal like a wounded husband, judges sin truly, yet promises mercy greater than His wrath.
options.note: The chapter holds together God's just judgment and His restoring grace.

options.text: He is indifferent to whether His people are faithful.
options.note: He is far from indifferent; unfaithfulness grieves Him deeply.

options.text: He is only angry and offers no hope.
options.note: Real anger is present, but the chapter ends in hope and restoration.

options.text: He changes His mind because He was mistaken.
options.note: His mercy is not a correction of error but the outworking of His steadfast love.

questions: God turned Hosea's whole household into a message. Where might God be asking you to let your ordinary life, not just your words, speak of Him?
Israel's idolatry is described as adultery against a faithful God. What lesser loves compete for the devotion you owe to the LORD?
The name Lo-ammi, not My people, is the most painful word in the chapter, yet it is the one grace most fully reverses. How does it move you that God turns outsiders into sons of the living God?
God announced restoration before the judgment even fell. How does knowing that His mercy runs ahead of His discipline shape the way you come back to Him after failure?
Peter says, once you had not received mercy, but now you have. How would living today in the light of that received mercy change the way you treat others?

translationNotes.note: Jezreel means God sows. The name first recalls the bloodshed by which Jehu's house took the throne, then is turned toward hope in verse 11.
Lo-ruhamah means she has not received mercy, or not pitied, from the root racham, tender compassion related to the word for womb.
Lo-ammi means not My people. A Hebrew reading of the final clause is I am not yours, sharpening the severing of the covenant bond.
Cited in Romans 9:26. The promise of offspring like the sand of the sea deliberately echoes the covenant with Abraham in Genesis 22:17.
